name: IV vitamin drip therapy

lead: IV vitamin drip therapy delivers fluids, vitamins and minerals directly into a vein. Clinics and mobile services market blends for hydration, hangover recovery, energy and a healthier-looking, glowing complexion, and the idea is that skin looks fresher when a person feels rested and hydrated.

The best-known blend is the Myers' cocktail, linked to Baltimore physician John Myers. Reference sources note that scientific evidence for its use as a general treatment is limited, and the practice is separate from medically indicated IV therapy.

paras: Sessions at clinics or by mobile providers involve a clinician placing an IV line and running a premixed bag over a period of time, with menus named for goals such as glow, hydration or recovery. Providers often offer add-ons such as additional vitamins.

Any IV carries risks of infection, vein irritation and fluid or electrolyte problems. Sports regulators prohibit larger-volume infusions in competition, and athletes have been suspended after boutique IV visits. The US FTC has sued a seller of IV products over false health claims.

angle.text: Providers market drips for a glowing complexion and recovery from late nights, on the premise that hydration and nutrients show in the skin.

lead: IV vitamin drip therapy, sometimes called boutique or wellness IV therapy, is the infusion of fluids with vitamins and minerals into the bloodstream, marketed for hydration, hangover relief, energy and skin 'glow'. [1][2]

The original reference formula is the Myers' cocktail, associated with John A. Myers, a Baltimore physician who reportedly gave vitamin infusions to patients before his death in 1984; physician Alan Gaby later published the commonly cited recipe. [2] A first boutique IV clinic reportedly opened in Tokyo in 2008, and celebrity customers publicised the clinics in the 2010s. [1]
Reference sources state that scientific evidence supporting Myers' cocktail as a treatment is limited and that Quackwatch lists it among questionable treatments. [2]
infobox: State medical rules; FTC for advertising claims

paras: Medical IV therapy is used for acute situations such as alcohol toxicity, where electrolytes and vitamins are replaced. Boutique IV clinics extend this to elective wellness use. [1] Elle described the target market as health enthusiasts who also drink heavily. [1]

The World Anti-Doping Agency prohibits IV infusions over 100 mL per 12 hours without a medical exemption, and USADA has warned that IVs can change blood test results. [1] Footballer Samir Nasri (2017) and swimmer Ryan Lochte (2018) were suspended after clinic visits. [1] In 2018 the US Federal Trade Commission sued a seller of Myers' cocktails and other IV treatments over false health claims. [2]
